Medical History

- Current health concerns and risk factors:  Acute left-sided throbbing headache began today at mid-day; preceded by zig-zag visual aura and blurred vision; associated photophobia, nausea, and two episodes of vomiting. Similar episode a few weeks ago. Uses combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) for 3 months (thrombotic risk). High occupational stress; minimal physical activity.  
- Relevant family medical history:  Mother has migraines and hypothyroidism; no known family brain tumors.  
- Medications (including OTC or shared medications):  Microgynon (combined oral contraceptive) – dose/route/frequency not documented. Occasional use of over-the-counter analgesics during prior headache (specific agents/doses not documented).  
- Immunisation status reviewed:  Not recorded.  
- Sexual and reproductive health:  Sexually active; on COCP for contraception. No further sexual history recorded.  
- Physical activity and nutrition:  Reports no regular exercise; diet not discussed.  
- Alcohol, tobacco, and substance use:  Denies smoking and alcohol use; no other substance use recorded.  
- Hearing loss or concerns:  Not recorded.  
- Mood/mental health (including depression, self-harm risk):  Feels stressed due to work pressure; denies low mood. No self-harm ideation reported.  
- Vision problems or recent changes:  Transient zig-zag visual aura and blurred vision before headache; photophobia.  
- Family and social relationships, caring responsibilities:  Lives alone; works in fashion industry with high stress; no caring responsibilities noted.

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• Classical features of migraine with aura: unilateral throbbing pain, visual aura, photophobia, nausea/vomiting, positive family history, similar prior episode.  
• No red-flag neurologic deficits, fever, rash, or trauma.  
• Risk factor for thrombotic headache disorders (estrogen COCP).  

Differential diagnoses (consistent with transcript and DDx)  
1. Migraine with visual aura – High likelihood; symptom constellation and family history.  
2. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – Moderate likelihood; new severe headache, worse on bending forward, recent COCP initiation.  
3. Intracranial mass/tumor – Low likelihood; positional worsening and vomiting but lacks progressive course or focal signs.

Working diagnosis: Migraine with visual aura.  
Plan: Symptomatic treatment today; monitor for red-flag symptoms; consider further evaluation if headaches persist or worsen.

Management Plan

- Provided education that presentation most consistent with migraine; reassured patient regarding low likelihood of brain tumor.  
- Advised analgesia: Paracetamol, or Co-codamol; consider NSAIDs such as Ibuprofen or Naproxen (doses not specified).  
- Recommended keeping a headache diary to identify triggers and frequency.  
- Discussed possibility of prophylactic migraine medication if attacks become frequent; review next week.  
- Safety-net advice: return urgently if headache worsens, unresponsive to medication, or develops focal neurologic symptoms, visual changes, worsening neck pain, or other concerning signs.  
- Follow-up appointment arranged for next week.

Consider:

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits):  Not recorded.  
- Reproductive or sexual health clinic referral:  Not recorded.  
- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support):  Not recorded (patient currently coping; mild stress only).  
- CTG registration:  Not recorded.  
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test):  Not recorded.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):

1. Migraine with visual aura – High likelihood: fits unilateral throbbing pain, visual aura, photophobia, nausea/vomiting, family history; no focal deficits.  
2. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – Moderate likelihood: recent estrogen COCP use and positional worsening; lacks focal signs but considered due to risk.  
3. Intracranial mass / brain tumor – Low likelihood: headache with vomiting and positional element but acute, non-progressive course makes this less probable.

Quality checks (always include at bottom of note):

● Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs (BP, pulse), BMI/weight, comprehensive neurological examination findings, immunisation review, alcohol/smoking quantities, full sexual history, dietary assessment, urinalysis, basic vision and ear exams, routine blood tests.  
● No internal contradictions noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: clear narrative but lacked documented physical examination and objective data.
